transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

At work my mind jumps to every little thing going on around me, and I lose track of what I’m doing in the middle of a customer call. It’s gotten to the point where I was just placed on a performance improvement plan at my call center, and I'm terrified of losing my job. That's really why I'm here today to get some help.
Do you find that these worries or distractions are limited to your work performance, or do they also affect other areas of your life, such as your relationships or daily activities?

They definitely spill over at home, and it's caused a lot of tension with my wife because I constantly forget bills, chores, and appointments unless they're right in front of me. Even when I try to relax, I can't just sit still to watch a movie or read, and I end up bouncing around starting DIY projects that I never actually finish. My wife ends up having to quietly pick up all the slack, which isn't fair to her.
Can you tell me more about your behavior as a child, did you have similar difficulties with sitting still, following instructions, or completing tasks when you were in school?

Yes, this actually goes all the way back to elementary school. My teachers used to move my seat constantly because I wouldn't stop talking or tapping my pencil, and I'd stare out the window instead of finishing worksheets. My report cards always said I was smart, but that I "didn't pay attention" and "rushed and made careless mistakes."
Did you often interrupt others, blurt out answers, or have difficulty waiting for your turn in class or in social situations when you were a child?

To be honest, I don't specifically remember if I had trouble waiting my turn or interrupted others back then. I do clearly remember my teachers constantly complaining about me talking too much and never sitting still, though.
Can you think of any situations, either now or when you were younger, where you felt extremely restless or fidgety, like you just couldn't keep still, even when you were supposed to be quiet or calm?

Yes, absolutely, both now and when I was a kid. During long meetings at work, I get this buzzing feeling inside like I'm trapped, so I'm constantly jiggling my leg, clicking my pen, or fiddling with my phone just to get through them. It’s the same way I felt in elementary school, where my teachers had to move my seat because I couldn't stop tapping my pencil or talking when we were supposed to be quiet.
Have you ever found yourself so intensely focused on a task or activity that you lost track of time and neglected other responsibilities or activities around you?

I don't really experience that kind of deep, intense focus. For me, it's actually the opposite—my mind is constantly jumping around, and I get so easily distracted that I just bounce from one unfinished task to another.
Have you ever had any activities or tasks where you were so focused that you didn't notice what was going on around you and lost track of time?

No, I really don't experience that at all. My mind is always doing the exact opposite, where it's constantly jumping from one thing to another and getting easily distracted. I've never been able to get so absorbed in a task that I tune out the world around me.

You mentioned you've never experienced being so focused on a task that you lost track of time, but can you think of any activities, even hobbies, where you might feel more engaged or less distracted than in your daily tasks or work?

I can't really think of any activities where I'm less distracted. Even with hobbies like DIY projects or trying to watch a movie, I get distracted, leave things unfinished, or feel the need to jump to something else.

Is it possible that there are certain activities, perhaps those that are highly stimulating or very interesting to you, where you might exhibit the opposite behavior, such as being overly focused or engaged to the point of ignoring other things around you?

No, I really don't experience that kind of intense hyperfocus at all. Instead of getting deeply absorbed in things, I'm usually the exact opposite—constantly distracted, restless, and bouncing from one unfinished task to another.
